instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 237 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 120.9, target 90.5. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 6.5, target 13.1. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 33.8, target 26.7. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 1.0, target 10.7. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 1.1, target 1.0. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 1.0. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 31.3, target 31.9. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 1.5, target 1.3. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be required to perform community service, and I hope you will consider making it a graduation requirement. Helping others teaches lessons that no classroom can fully deliver.

Consider the friends who tutor elementary school children. They learn patience, explain ideas they once found difficult, and discover that they are capable of teaching. Students who clean up litter along a city park learn that their actions affect the places where others live and play. These experiences build responsibility and empathy, qualities that employers and colleges value.

I understand the concern that service takes time away from homework, sports, jobs, and rest. However, a requirement of perhaps twenty hours spread across four years is modest. Students already spend hours on activities that serve only themselves, and a small commitment to others can broaden their perspective without overwhelming their schedules. Many students also find that the work they expected to dislike becomes the most meaningful part of their year.

To make the requirement fair, the school could offer a wide range of options, from tutoring and food drives to environmental cleanups and hospital volunteering, so that every student can find a placement that fits their interests and abilities.

Thank you for considering this proposal. I believe that a community is strengthened when its young people learn to give back, and our school is the right place to begin that lesson.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student
